prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Solar PV capacity additions by country and quarter, 2024 (MW) (language en).
Grid: 9 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes.
Merged cells: "Segment" spans 1 col × 3 row; "Europe" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Asia-Pacific" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Germany" spans 2 col × 1 row; "France" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Japan" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Australia" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Segment" · longest unbreakable unit 86px · widest one-line content 172px
  col 2: header "Europe › Germany › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 40px · widest one-line content 40px
  col 3: header "Europe › Germany › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 40px · widest one-line content 40px
  col 4: header "Europe › France › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 33px · widest one-line content 33px
  col 5: header "Europe › France › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 6: header "Asia-Pacific › Japan › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 7: header "Asia-Pacific › Japan › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 8: header "Asia-Pacific › Australia › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 28px · widest one-line content 28px
  col 9: header "Asia-Pacific › Australia › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 606px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). The table, including its 1px outer border, must be at most 606px wide (column widths sum to at most 605px); no horizontal scrolling. A table exactly 606px wide fits.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Several designers worked independently on this table. You see their final layouts, anonymised as Layout P, in that order after the overview: Layout P.
Measured facts:
Layout P: column widths [144, 61, 61, 54, 59, 59, 59, 49, 59] px · table 606×338 px · row heights [36, 36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 36, 36] · column headers on >1 line: 0/15 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · fits the 606 px viewport (no scrolling)

Compare them side by side. For each layout name its strengths, its faults and the spatial logic behind it (how it distributes space and why). Do not just pick a winner: you may combine the strengths of several layouts, propose something new, or overturn all of them. Propose up to 3 new designs that you expect to be better than every layout shown; if you believe one shown layout cannot be improved, say so in "best" and propose fewer or none.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"analysis":[{"layout":"name","strengths":"","faults":"","spatial_logic":""}],"insights":"what the comparison teaches about this table","best":["names of the best layout(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"idea":"what it combines or changes, and why"}]}

log.raw: {"analysis":[{"layout":"P","strengths":"All headers and values are visible, the geographic and country groupings are clear, and the table fits the viewport exactly. Numeric entries remain on one line, making quarter-to-quarter and country comparisons easy. The two longer segment labels wrap at natural word boundaries.","faults":"The first two data rows are taller than the others, and their labels take two lines.
